content: Human granulocytic anaplasmosis (HGA) is a disease caused by the bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum, an obligate intracellular gram-negative organism that infects neutrophils. This bacterium was previously known as Ehrlichia equi and Ehrlichia phagocytophilum. HGA is an emerging tick-borne illness in the United States and Europe, transmitted primarily by black-legged deer ticks (Ixodes scapularis) in the eastern and midwestern United States and Ixodes pacificus in the western United States. In Europe, Ixodes ricinus is the presumed vector. The disease is zoonotic, with white-tailed deer and white-footed mice serving as the primary animal reservoirs. The clinical presentation of HGA in humans is variable. Many cases are subclinical or present with mild symptoms such as fever, muscle aches (myalgia), and general malaise. These nonspecific symptoms make definitive diagnosis challenging. In symptomatic cases, fever, headache, myalgia, nausea, and vomiting are common. A rash, which may be macular, maculopapular, or petechial, occurs in less than 10% of patients. Neurological symptoms, such as neck stiffness and confusion, are less common. Severe complications, including seizures, coma, respiratory failure, renal failure, myocarditis, and opportunistic infections, can occur if left untreated. The case fatality rate is low, at less than 1%. The life cycle of the tick vector involves several stages. Adult female ticks lay eggs in the spring, which hatch into six-legged larvae. These larvae feed on small mammals or birds, often becoming infected with Anaplasma phagocytophilum. The larvae then molt into eight-legged nymphs, which remain dormant during the fall and winter. In the spring, nymphs feed on larger hosts, such as deer, humans, or dogs, and can transmit the bacterium. Nymphs then molt into adult ticks, which mate and lay eggs, completing the cycle. After a tick bite, Anaplasma phagocytophilum enters the bloodstream through the dermis. Bacteremia typically develops 4–7 days after the bite. The bacterium primarily infects granulocytes, including neutrophils, eosinophils, and monocytes. It evades the immune system by inhibiting phagosome-lysosome fusion and suppressing the respiratory burst of neutrophils, thereby preventing the release of reactive oxygen species. Additionally, it delays neutrophil apoptosis, allowing the bacterium to survive and replicate within the host cells. HGA is most commonly reported in the upper midwestern and northeastern United States, with the highest incidence in states such as Vermont, Maine, Rhode Island, Minnesota, Massachusetts, Wisconsin, New Hampshire, and New York. The disease is most prevalent during the summer months, particularly in June and July, coinciding with the peak activity of nymphal ticks. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV, cancer, or organ transplants, are at higher risk of severe disease and mortality. Diagnosis of HGA is often presumptive, based on clinical presentation, history of tick exposure, and laboratory findings. Common laboratory abnormalities include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated levels of aminotransferases, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase. Serological tests, such as the indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) test, are used to confirm the diagnosis. A fourfold rise in anti-IgG antibodies against Anaplasma phagocytophilum is indicative of current or past infection. The sensitivity of the IFA test is approximately 95%. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is also used but is less sensitive. Blood cultures are not useful for diagnosing HGA. Treatment is indicated for all symptomatic patients. The preferred regimen is doxycycline, 100 mg orally or intravenously twice daily for 10 days. For patients with mild illness who cannot tolerate doxycycline due to drug allergy, pregnancy, or age under 8 years, rifampin (300 mg orally twice daily for 7–10 days) is an alternative. Pediatric patients aged 8 years or older can be treated with doxycycline at 4 mg/kg/day (maximum 100 mg per dose) for 10 days. For children under 8 years or pregnant women, rifampin is the preferred treatment. If the patient has concurrent Lyme disease, amoxicillin or cefuroxime axetil should be initiated after completing the doxycycline course to ensure a 14-day total antibiotic regimen. Rifampin is not effective for Lyme disease, so co-infected patients should receive appropriate treatment for both infections. Prognosis is excellent for patients who receive timely treatment, with symptoms typically resolving within 48 hours of initiating doxycycline or rifampin. Untreated patients may experience bacteremia for up to 30 days and prolonged symptoms, but all patients recover within 60 days regardless of antibiotic therapy. The mortality rate is approximately 1%. Primary prevention of HGA involves avoiding tick exposure. This includes using insect repellents containing DEET or permethrin, wearing protective clothing, thoroughly bathing after outdoor activities, and promptly removing ticks from the skin. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended, and no vaccine is currently available for HGA prevention.
